title: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father
description: Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to
body: Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

schema.headline: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father

title: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast
description: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nat
body: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes."There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us."The wildlife will approach you sometimes."Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular."In theory, they should have migrated."Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks. Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.

schema.headline: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president says he is backed by 'vast majority' in world football
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether h
body: Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof"."There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on."Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016. The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of competitions run by football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm.Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable.He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it"."We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world."I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view. "But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority."I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football]  countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations.England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine.This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually.Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves."It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said."When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president says he is backed by 'vast majority' in world football

title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
description: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailer
body: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say. AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist, external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

schema.headline: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

title: Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron home
description: The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacin
body: The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".Hebron's Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said more than 1,000 people had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.He said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment. Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene."We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said. He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory. In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.Speaking to journalists, Hebron's mayor said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

schema.headline: Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron home

title: Northern Olympics plan to get £7m in John Healey's first Budget
description: The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how diffe
body: The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost £8.9bn.A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a £9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable."Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport."We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement."Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

schema.headline: Northern Olympics plan to get £7m in John Healey's first Budget

title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
description: Image source, ReutersBySareen HabeshianLos AngelesFew places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for gl
body: Image source, ReutersBySareen HabeshianLos AngelesFew places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to the rich and famous.Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades."I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill."If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.Image source, Getty ImagesWhile the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth taxMeta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy."I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule". "They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy."This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".Correction 24 October: An earlier version of this article contained a graphic which incorrectly said median income in California was $288,000. This has been corrected to median household net worth.

schema.headline: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?

title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale
description: Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive St
body: Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices."They're getting changed," he said on Instagram."It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front."The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said."I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future. Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale

title: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?
description: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fun
body: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries? One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate. The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries. And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes. If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows. However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK? Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund. But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.But there are two issues to consider. Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes). Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing. As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap. The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men. But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere. But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action. The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?

title: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
description: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband saysImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island
body: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband saysImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of Leanne Gregory on TuesdayByBen CarrEast MidlandsUpdated 4 hours agoThe husband of a British woman who died rescuing their sons when they were swept away to sea in the Bahamas says she was a "hero... in life and in death".Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been snorkelling with her family when the boys were swept away by a strong current, police said. Although the children were rescued from the water off the island of Bimini on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.Nathan Gregory said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable for our family".'Absolute hero'"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post."I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together."My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and  totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."Image source, NurPhoto/Getty ImagesImage caption, The two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas saidIn a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers  received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.Mrs Gregory was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas."We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Nottingham

schema.headline: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas

title: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?
description: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?Image caption, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess
body: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?Image caption, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman's "keep dancing" move for threeByIan YoungsCulture reporterStrictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.Image caption, The new hosts joined the judges on the dance floor when the series beganAfter they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding."Metro's Adam Miller said, external their debut was "a triumph", however, and the i Paper's Sarah Carson wrote, external that Strictly had "played a blinder", even though the hosts "looked a little awkward as a three at times".Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external.And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem."He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News."I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."Image caption, Widdicombe has been at the centre of comic sketches with the other hosts and judgesThe problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous."They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in."Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him"."But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.Image caption, Emma Willis has hosted shows including Big Brother and The VoiceRadio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in."I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less."They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds."It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly."Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."Image caption, One episode featured Widdicombe and Willis in a Mary Poppins-inspired sketchFrost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests."Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".Image source, Guy Levy / Ray Burmiston / BBCImage caption, Radebe has already gained a reputation for his flamboyant fashionBut while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain."JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast."He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable."And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.Image caption, The presenting trio watched on as Dame Sarah Storey and dance partner Julian Caillon were eliminated last weekendDr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled"."I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says."He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well."Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell."And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

schema.headline: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?

title: Tottenham Hotspur: Are Roberto de Zerbi's side finally on their way back after win at Chelsea?
description: Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th
body: Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th in the Premier League - their highest league position since 2 January.And, after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes, there are growing signs Roberto de Zerbi's side are showing there is real light at the end of a pretty dark tunnel.Saturday's impressive win at Stamford Bridge was just the second time they have won two league games in a row in 42 attempts - inspired by starring roles from James Maddison and Mathys Tel.It was also the first time they have enjoyed as much as 68% possession in a match since April 2025.The win was deserved too, although Chelsea certainly gave them a helping hand with goalkeeper Mike Penders punching the opener into his own net and Cole Palmer sent off for two yellow cards.Spurs had taken seven attempts to get their first league win of the season against Coventry on Monday and on Saturday they looked transformed from the side that did not even score a goal until September 1.It left De Zerbi glowing with positivity, despite another injury setback for Maddison, as he highlighted a team meeting earlier this month that sparked their revival in fortunes."Seven points after Manchester, before Manchester we spoke a lot, we had a big meeting" he said. "We removed the masks and spoke honestly and clearly in front of ourselves. From that moment, I think something started to change within us."I think we have put something different into Tottenham in the last period. Not a different attitude, but different relationships with the players, different relationships within the group."We have changed the spirit of the group and improved the performances of the players, especially some of the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We have suffered enough."Former Chelsea goalkeeper Rob Green added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A dream afternoon for Tottenham. They looked controlled, looked at ease, they looked like they were comfortable on the ball."Results like this galvanise a side. When you look at the players coming back, yes Maddison got injured and he'll be a question mark over the next few weeks, but players coming back, momentum coming back - you feel, and say it quietly, Tottenham might just be coming back."Italian De Zerbi was appointed Spurs boss at the end of March 2026 with the club in crisis.He arrived as the club's third manager of the campaign and, with seven games remaining, Tottenham were just one point clear of the drop zone.After securing safety, albeit after a few scares, the club spent more than £300m on summer signings for the first time in their history as they backed De Zerbi to restore them to former glories.And, after a slow start to the campaign and still lacking firepower in attack, the long-suffering Tottenham fans will be left feeling more positive than they have done for a long time."Tottenham have made a big statement in a really convincing performance," former Arsenal defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport."I thought Maddison was magnificent in midfield. He's like the Artful Dodger, isn't he? That midfield is full of mischief, but he's brave against the ball."I thought Tel was magnificent out on the left-hand side, [Mohammed] Kudus on the right was also really effective, and everybody really managed to handle the ball really well on the night. "Spurs had almost 70% possession, which is remarkable for a team which was just a few places from the bottom of the table. I think what's changed for Spurs is the key personnel."De Zerbi ran on to the pitch to celebrate with the travelling supporters at the final whistle, while his coaches and substitutes raced towards the players in the corner of the ground.He has previously spoken of how he inherited players that cried after matches and lost all confidence - and believed his unprecedented control over the summer transfers was vindication for Spurs from last season.It was fitting that Tel, who has attracted criticism from his own supporters since arriving from Bayern Munich for £30m in June 2025, provided the decisive moment to seal just a second league success in 36 years at Chelsea - a stunning low finish after a driving run.The French forward, 21, told Sky Sports: "It is very special because we have come to Chelsea so many times and not got a win. We showed great mentality today and we need to enjoy this win."We created a lot of chances today. We walk out together, the goal is something special for me, I'm happy about it and let's keep pushing now."Summer signing Matheus Fernandes added: "We are here to change the club's mentality, we want to beat the top teams, and make this victory for the fans."In the summer, Spurs twice broke their transfer record with three of their first signings, as they added centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton, Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle.And all three impressed De Zerbi against Chelsea as he added: "Jan Paul van Hecke played very well, Matheus Fernandes played very well, Sandro Tonali played very well."I think it was Tonali's best game since joining Tottenham. Omar Marmoush played a good game. It was a tough game for him, but he fought in the right way."Mathys Tel played very well too. I think we won the game with our two wingers, Mohammed Kudus and Mathys Tel. They made the difference."It was notable Fernandes, 22, was criticised by his manager last month.The return of Maddison, who missed almost all of last season with a serious knee injury, was key in Monday's 3-1 home victory over Coventry City - and he again looked impressive before being withdrawn in the second half with a suspected groin injury."I don't think it is a very important problem," said De Zerbi. "I hope it is not a big problem. He is a special player for us. We need him."Maddison is part of a returning group of players, including Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski, who are making comebacks from lengthy absences.Spurs are now unbeaten in three games, with back-to-back victories following the 1-1 draw at Manchester United in which they were arguably the better side.As well as the team meeting before the Old Trafford encounter, Spurs enjoyed a warm-weather training camp in Marbella, where heavyweight boxer Anthony Joshua paid them a visit.It feels as though some semblance of the old Spurs is returning, although they remain unconvincing in attack with just eight goals in as many games.Manchester City loanee Marmoush misfired again and his replacement Dominic Solanke was underwhelming in previous matches, while Richarlison has been frozen out in the reserves after being left out of their Premier League squad.But after this notable derby victory at Chelsea - earning a clean sheet there too for the first time since 1986 - it felt like the first part of De Zerbi's rebuild is well under way.

schema.headline: Tottenham Hotspur: Are Roberto de Zerbi's side finally on their way back after win at Chelsea?

title: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams
description: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been st
body: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work."It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat."That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music"."When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album."I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline. "When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says. "There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad."There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic. "I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland."We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track"."I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well. "So there's a little message from me in each song."

schema.headline: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams
